title: Checkout footer visibility now applies to merchant-configurable content
summary:
The visibility fields on CheckoutBrandingFooterContent and CheckoutAndAccountsConfigurationBrandingFooterContent now control only merchant-configurable footer content. Checkout can display Shopify-provided transaction information in the footer regardless of this setting. Existing apps don’t need to change their GraphQL Admin API requests, but apps that preview or test checkout branding shouldn’t assume that HIDDEN produces an empty footer.

What changed

Checkout can now display Shopify-provided copy in the footer for eligible orders. This content is part of checkout and isn’t controlled by the footer content visibility setting or configurable through checkout branding.

The visibility setting continues to control merchant-configurable footer content, including merchant policy links and copyright copy. Setting it to HIDDEN hides that merchant-configurable content without suppressing Shopify-provided footer content.

The descriptions for the following GraphQL Admin API fields now clarify this boundary:

  • CheckoutBrandingFooterContent.visibility
  • CheckoutBrandingFooterContentInput.visibility
  • CheckoutAndAccountsConfigurationBrandingFooterContent.visibility
  • CheckoutAndAccountsConfigurationBrandingFooterContentInput.visibility

No fields, input types, enum values, access scopes, or mutations have changed.

Who's affected

This change affects apps that customize checkout branding for Shopify Plus stores through either the legacy Checkout Branding API or the Checkout and Accounts Configuration API, especially if they manage footer visibility or render previews.

All checkouts and Thank You pages now display the additional Shopify-provided footer copy. Apps that don’t manage checkout footer visibility are unaffected.

The clarification applies to every GraphQL Admin API version where the corresponding branding type exists. It isn’t tied to a new API version.

Why this matters

This change clarifies the boundary between merchant-configurable branding and content that checkout provides. You can continue controlling merchant policy and copyright content while checkout presents relevant order context in the footer without changing the main checkout layout.

Branding previews and automated tests can now treat Shopify-provided footer content separately from merchant-configurable content, so you can represent the rendered checkout footer more accurately.

What to do

No action is required to keep existing integrations working. Existing mutations and stored branding configurations continue to work without changes.

If your app manages or previews checkout branding:

  1. Check whether it assumes that visibility: HIDDEN removes all footer content.
  2. Update previews and visual tests to allow Shopify-provided transaction information to remain visible when visibility hides only merchant-configurable content.

title: Hydrogen 2026-10 is now available
summary:
The new Hydrogen is generally available today. Since the developer preview started in June, we've shipped seven releases based on feedback from developers using it.

The big deal about the new Hydrogen is that it isn't a big deal: Hydrogen now works with any JavaScript framework. You can bring Shopify's commerce to your stack just by adding the library to your app, instead of needing to replatform.

Hydrogen then handles commerce for you: the cart, variant selection, prices in the buyer's currency, analytics that respect consent, Shop Pay, and customer login. React Router and Next.js have starters ready to deploy, and you can host it anywhere, including Oxygen, which is still free.

The package also includes skills that teach coding agents how to use it. To try it in an existing project, run npx @shopify/hydrogen@latest setup and ask your agent to "Set up my store with Shopify."

What Hydrogen gives you

Every Shopify storefront needs the same commerce pieces, and they're harder to get right than they look. The cart has to stay correct when a shopper taps "Add to cart" twice. Prices have to match the buyer's country and currency. Analytics have to respect consent and still reach Shopify, or your reports go quiet.

Hydrogen handles those for you: the cart, product variants, collection filters, predictive search, Markets, analytics, Shop Pay, and customer accounts. Your framework keeps routing, data loading, and rendering, and the design is all yours.

The glue code fits in a few lines. For instance, a dynamically updating cart count in React looks like this:

import { createCartComponents } from "@shopify/hydrogen/react";

const { CartProvider, useCart } = createCartComponents();

function CartCount() {
  const count = useCart((cart) => cart.data.totalQuantity);
  return {count};
}

Vue has the same thing as a composable, and other frameworks subscribe to the cart directly.

Built for coding agents

Hydrogen comes with 20 skills that teach coding agents how to use it, covering each part of a storefront. We wrote them by building storefronts with agents and fixing the skill every time an agent got something wrong. Ask your agent to "Set up my store with Shopify," and it builds the home, collection, search, product, cart, and account pages, adds analytics, and smoke-tests the result.

The skills live in your project and match the version of Hydrogen you installed, so your agent follows instructions for the code you actually have. After you upgrade Hydrogen versions, you can update the skills with npx @shopify/hydrogen skills sync.

Hydrogen storefronts also work with shopping agents. In browsers that support WebMCP, an agent can search your catalog and update the cart, and after the buyer confirms, Shopify Checkout can submit the order with complete_checkout. You don't have to build anything for it.

Hydrogen uses the same standard storefront actions as Liquid themes, so compatible apps, storefront UI, and agents can share the same cart contract. An app or agent adds to the cart by calling the same action your own UI uses:

await window.Shopify.actions.updateCart({
  lines: [{ merchandiseId: "gid://shopify/ProductVariant/123", quantity: 1 }],
});

If you've used Hydrogen before

Hydrogen used to be a framework built on React Router. To use its cart or analytics, you built your whole storefront on it. Now it's a library, so you can add it to the framework you already use and host it wherever you want. Oxygen is still free.

Existing Hydrogen storefronts keep working as they do now, and there's nothing you need to do today. When you're ready to move, the migration skill walks your agent through it. You keep your pages and routes and swap where the commerce code comes from.

Get started

There are a few ways to get started:

  • Run npx @shopify/hydrogen@latest setup in your own project.
  • Deploy the React Router template to Oxygen from your Shopify admin.
  • If you use Next.js, clone Vercel Shop, a storefront built on Hydrogen and maintained by Vercel.

If something's missing or broken, tell us in the Shopify developer community. The code is on GitHub, and the docs are on shopify.dev.

title: Add shopping and Shop Pay checkout to any agent with Shop MCP
summary:
Shop MCP lets your agent or app search Shopify Catalog, build carts, and complete Shop Pay checkout through a single MCP connection. It works with over 1 billion products in Shopify Catalog and doesn't require an API key for search. Nothing changes for existing Catalog API integrations, and no action is required.

What changed

Shop MCP is live at https://mcp.shop.com, with a skill description at https://mcp.shop.com/skill.md that MCP-compatible agents can read. One connection gives your agent 17 tools, grouped into a few main flows:

  • Search and product details: search_catalog, lookup_catalog, and get_product read from Shopify Catalog.
  • Sign-in with Shop: the shopper signs in once, and search tools use their saved sizes and preferences.
  • Carts and checkout on Shopify stores: your agent builds a cart and creates a checkout at the store that sells the product. Carts and checkout work without sign-in. With a signed-in shopper, checkout can use their saved addresses and Shop Pay, and your agent completes the purchase with complete_checkout after the shopper confirms the total and payment method.
  • Checkout on non-Shopify stores: when the store doesn't run on Shopify, the shopper approves the purchase in Shop, and your agent receives single-use card details to pay on the store's own checkout.
  • Orders: for a signed-in shopper, your agent finds orders and tracking with search_orders.

The shop CLI calls the same server from your terminal so you can try a search before you write any code:

npm install -g @shopify/shop
shop search "ceramic coffee dripper"

Each result shows the store, the price, and whether it's in stock. Replace the query with a product your agent sells to see the shape of the data your agent receives.

Orders placed through your agent appear in the merchant's Shopify admin like any other order. There are no webhooks at launch, so you need to poll get_checkout for checkout status.

Who's affected

Developers who build or configure MCP-compatible agents or tools can use Shop MCP. If you use the existing Catalog API directly, your current integrations keep working without changes.

Why this matters

Before Shop MCP, your agent could find a product in Catalog but had to send the shopper to the store's website to pay, which often caused drop-off. Now a signed-in shopper can pay with the Shop Pay details they've already saved without leaving your agent.

What to do

No action is required for existing integrations. To start using Shop MCP:

  1. Install the shop CLI and run shop search with a query to check results from your terminal.
  2. Point your coding agent at https://mcp.shop.com/skill.md, or add https://mcp.shop.com as an MCP server in your agent's config.
  3. To pay with Shop Pay, have the shopper sign in with Shop. MCP clients such as Claude and ChatGPT run sign-in for you, and your own code can use the device flow.
  4. Test a purchase end to end. It worked if the checkout returns status: completed with an order.

Search works without credentials. For higher rate limits, create an API key in the Shopify Dev Dashboard.

Related docs

  • Shop MCP overview
  • Global Catalog MCP

title: Cart updates that result in no changes to the cart no longer trigger carts/update webhooks
summary:
Cart operations that leave the cart unchanged, for example, resubmitting the same values a cart already has, no longer trigger a carts/update webhook. Shopify sends a webhook every time a cart's contents or properties change.

Previously, every cart operation produced a carts/update webhook. This change removes the duplicate notifications, and apps receive one carts/update for each change to a cart instead of one per request.

title: Detect when a POS extension screen finishes navigating
summary:
What changed

The POS Navigation API adds the navigatesuccess event. It fires after the destination screen finishes its native transition, and its callback receives a standard Event.

currententrychange can fire before the screen finishes appearing, and the navigate() promise doesn’t wait for the transition. When navigating back, register the listener on the screen that will reappear; the screen being left is removed.

Who’s affected

The event is available to POS UI extensions that target API version 2026-10 and run on POS builds that support it. Older POS builds won’t emit navigatesuccess.

What to do

No migration is required. To act after a screen finishes appearing, listen for navigatesuccess. Don’t use the navigate() promise as a signal that the native transition has finished.

title: Identify the published version running in a POS extension
summary:
What changed

shopify.extension.version returns the version of the extension that is running. It’s the same name shown on the Versions page in the Dev Dashboard and chosen when running shopify app deploy.

The value is an opaque name, not a version number, so compare it for equality rather than sorting it. It’s undefined when the extension runs from a local development server.

Who’s affected

This field is available to POS UI extensions that target API version 2026-10. Extensions targeting earlier API versions are unchanged.

Why this matters

POS can cache extension bundles and run them offline. The field helps developers identify which published build a merchant’s device is running.

What to do

No action is required for existing extensions. To use the field, target API version 2026-10. Account for undefined when testing from a local development server.

title: Catalog API now returns compare-at prices as `list_price`
summary:
The Catalog API now returns a merchant’s compare-at price as list_price on each product variant. Your app or agent can use list_price to tell when a product is marked down and by how much. The price field doesn’t change. No action is required.

list_price is an optional field defined in the UCP catalog specification, version 2026-08-25. It uses the same Price object as price, with amount in minor units and a currency. Products also return list_price_range, which includes the lowest and highest list_price across their variants.

A variant includes list_price when all of the following are true:

  • The merchant shares compare-at prices through Catalog Mapping in the Shopify admin. Shopify turns this on by default for most stores and turns it off for stores that use compare-at for MSRP or another reference price.
  • The compare-at price is higher than price for the buyer’s context.
  • The merchant shows compare-at prices in the buyer’s region. Stores that hide them from EEA buyers don’t return list_price to those buyers.

When list_price is missing, the variant has no compare-at price to show for that buyer and configuration. How you present that in your UI or in an agent’s response is up to you.

Learn how list_price appears in Global Catalog responses.

title: New `owner_type` field for metafield declarations in Checkout and Customer Account UI extensions, required in 2027-01
summary:
Starting with API version 2026-10, Checkout and Customer Account UI extensions can specify an owner_type for each metafield declaration in shopify.extension.toml. Starting with API version 2027-01, owner_type is required for every metafield declaration, and deployments without it will be blocked.

What changed

Metafield declarations in [[extensions.metafields]] and [[extensions.targeting.metafields]] accept a new owner_type property. owner_type names the resource that owns the metafield, such as PRODUCT or CUSTOMER.

Shopify uses owner_type to fetch only the metafields from the resource types your extension needs, which improves extension performance. On API version 2027-01 and later, every metafield declaration must include owner_type.

Who's affected

Checkout and Customer Account UI extensions that declare metafields in shopify.extension.toml and use API version 2027-01 or later are affected.

Extensions that don't declare metafields in shopify.extension.toml are unaffected.

What to do

On API version 2027-01 or later, deployments will be blocked if any metafield declaration is missing an owner_type. Add owner_type to each metafield declaration before you upgrade. You can add it now on 2026-10.

To migrate:

  1. Open your extension's shopify.extension.toml file and add the appropriate owner_type value for each metafield declaration.
  2. If your extension needs the same namespace and key from multiple resource types, create a separate declaration for each owner_type.
  3. Redeploy the extension and confirm that the deployment completes without validation errors related to metafield declarations.

title: Shopify Flow: Flow Trigger Lifecycle Callback extensions now support relative url paths
summary:
What's changed

Flow Trigger Lifecycle Callback extensions now support relative URLs in addition to absolute HTTPS URLs. This works similarly to relative URLs with Flow action extensions. Running app dev resolves your relative URL against your development tunnel URL and app deploy resolves against your app's application_url

Previously, the URL for Flow trigger lifecycle callback extensions were required to be absolute HTTPS URLs pointing to a web server. This required an already hosted system which made it inconvenient to test locally before deployment. Additionally, it required that the full URL be updated in addition to a Shopify app's application_url when being used with a dynamically tunneled server whose URL might change.

How it works

Use an absolute HTTPS URL when your endpoint is hosted outside your app or you want Flow to call the same URL in every environment.

Protocol-relative URLs (such as //example.com/api/execute) aren't supported, and your app configuration must include an absolute HTTPS application_url before you deploy with relative paths.

For more details, see the Flow trigger lifecycle callback configuration reference.

title: Cart mutations reject unconfirmed writes in POS UI extensions 2026-10
summary:
In POS UI extensions API version 2026-10, Cart API mutations reject when Shopify POS doesn't confirm that the cart changed. In earlier versions these mutations resolve whether or not POS applied the write. This is a breaking change for apps that adopt 2026-10, and those apps need to handle a rejected promise on every cart mutation they call. Apps on 2026-07 and earlier are unaffected.

What changed

POS reports the outcome of every cart write. Only a success result confirms that the cart changed. Earlier API versions resolve the mutation regardless of that result, so an app can't tell an applied write from a dropped one, and an app can show a fee or a discount as applied when the cart never changed.

In 2026-10, these mutations reject unless POS confirms the write: bulkCartUpdate, removeLineItem, applyCartDiscount, addCartCodeDiscount, removeAllDiscounts, setCustomer, removeCustomer, addLineItemProperties, bulkAddLineItemProperties, removeLineItemProperties, setLineItemDiscount, bulkSetLineItemDiscounts, removeLineItemDiscount, addLineItemSellingPlan, and removeLineItemSellingPlan. updateLineItemQuantity is new in 2026-10 and rejects from its first release.

An unconfirmed write rejects with one of two messages:

  • POS refused the cart update. The cart was not changed. POS declined the write and the cart is unchanged. This can happen when POS is no longer accepting cart changes, for example after the cashier moves to payment. Retrying can succeed once cart editing is available again.
  • POS could not confirm the cart update. The outcome is unknown and a partial write is possible. Read the cart before you retry.

These two messages cover unconfirmed writes. A cart mutation can still reject for other reasons, such as an invalid discount value or a missing customer, so match on the message only when you need to tell the two cases apart.

Who's affected

Apps that call any of the mutations above from a POS UI extension with api_version = "2026-10" or later. The change applies per extension, based on the API version the extension declares, not per store.

Apps on 2026-07 and earlier keep the current behavior with no changes. Apps that already wrap cart mutations in try/catch or attach a .catch() handler run that handler on an unconfirmed write instead of continuing as though the write succeeded.

Why this matters

A dropped cart write is silent today. Rejection turns that silent data loss into an error at the call site, where an app can retry, surface a message to the staff, or roll back its own state.

Breaking changes and migrations

Caution: Calls that previously resolved now reject. If a rejection isn't caught, the rest of your handler doesn't run, including any UI you render after the write and any cleanup such as clearing a loading state.

Handle rejection at each call site before you bump an extension to 2026-10.

Before:

await shopify.cart.applyCartDiscount('FixedAmount', 'Winter discount', '5.00');
setDiscountApplied(true);

After:

try {
  await shopify.cart.applyCartDiscount('FixedAmount', 'Winter discount', '5.00');
  setDiscountApplied(true);
} catch (error) {
  setDiscountApplied(false);
  showToast('Could not update the cart. Try again before payment.');
}

If you can't migrate immediately, keep the extension on 2026-07 or earlier. Those versions aren't affected, and you can bump after the handling is in place.

Action required

Add rejection handling to every cart mutation your extension calls, then set api_version = "2026-10". Apps that bump without handling rejection will see handlers stop at the first unconfirmed write, which can leave a spinner on screen or skip a confirmation step. 2026-07 continues to work until it reaches the end of its support window under API versioning.

  • API versioning

title: POS UI extensions now return percentage values for percentage discounts
summary:
Shopify POS 11.15 corrects the value returned by Discount.amount for Percentage discounts to match the Cart API contract. Extensions that used this value as money need to update their logic.

What changed

A 25% discount on a $200 line item now returns amount: 25. POS 11.14 and earlier returned amount: 50, the monetary amount deducted.

This applies to cart-level and line-item percentage discounts, including manual, app-applied, and automatic discounts exposed with type: 'Percentage'. It affects the Cart API's current state and subscriptions, lineItems[].discounts, cartDiscount, cartDiscounts, and the cartLineItem contextual API.

This fix also prevents a percentage discount's monetary allocation from being reinterpreted as a percentage when an extension passes cart state back through bulkCartUpdate.

FixedAmount and Code discounts are unchanged, including percentage-based discount codes exposed with type: 'Code'.

Who's affected

The change applies to all POS UI extensions API versions. Keeping an older api_version does not preserve the previous behavior.

What to do

  1. Check Discount.type before interpreting amount, and update currency displays, savings calculations, loyalty points, and integrations that treat Percentage amounts as money.
  2. Test cart-level, line-item, and automatic percentage discounts, plus any bulkCartUpdate workflows, on POS 11.15 or later.
  3. If your extension supports POS 11.14 or earlier, handle the previous behavior until those devices are upgraded.

title: Per-customer request limit for the Customer Account API
summary:
The Customer Account API now enforces a per-customer rate limit of 3000 requests per minute per store, shared across all apps. This affects all apps that call the Customer Account API, but you typically don't need to make changes because normal buyer traffic stays well under this limit.

What changed

The Customer Account API now limits each customer on a store to 3000 requests per minute. This limit is shared across all apps installed on that store that call the Customer Account API. It applies in addition to the existing cost-based rate limit for the API.

When your app exceeds this per-customer limit, the API returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a THROTTLED error and a Retry-After header. For more details, see the Customer Account API rate limits documentation.

Who's affected

This change affects all apps that call the Customer Account API on any store. The per-customer limit applies regardless of which app makes the requests, since the limit is shared across all apps for a given customer and store.

What you should do

You don't need to take action in most cases, since normal buyer traffic should remain well under this per-customer limit.

If your app uses the Customer Account API, you should make sure its retry logic:

  1. Detects HTTP 429 responses.
  2. Reads the Retry-After header from the response.
  3. Waits for the duration in Retry-After, then retries the request.

title: Downgrade app access scopes from write to read
summary:
Starting with Admin GraphQL API version 2027-01, apps that use Shopify-managed installation can call appDowngradeAccessScopes to replace optional write scopes with their matching read scopes. No action is required for existing apps.

What changed

The mutation affects only the calling app’s installation. Requested scopes must be declared in optional_scopes and must be write scopes with matching read scopes. Required scopes can’t be downgraded. Write scopes that aren’t currently granted are ignored. If any requested scope fails validation, the request is rejected and the installation’s scopes remain unchanged.

Revoking a write scope with appRevokeAccessScopes also removes its read access when the read scope was only granted through the write scope. Use appDowngradeAccessScopes when your app still needs that read access.

Who’s affected

This change applies to apps that use Shopify-managed installation and declare optional write scopes with corresponding read scopes. The mutation is available starting with Admin GraphQL API version 2027-01.

What to do

If your app no longer needs write access, call appDowngradeAccessScopes with the optional write scopes you want to downgrade. For example, downgrade write_products to read_products when your app no longer needs to create or update products:

mutation {
  appDowngradeAccessScopes(scopes: ["write_products"]) {
    downgraded {
      handle
    }
    userErrors {
      field
      message
    }
  }
}

The downgraded field returns the write scopes that were successfully changed. Check userErrors for any validation failures.

  • appDowngradeAccessScopes reference
  • API Access Scopes

title: What's new in Polaris 2.0.0-rc.1
summary:
Polaris 2.0.0-rc.1 brings more components in line with the new admin style update, fixes several layout and event-handling bugs, and improves mounting and update performance.

What's changed

Components

  • Table now matches the updated Shopify admin design.
  • Tooltip can now be placed in Section's supplemental slot.
  • Section now supports equal-height cards within the same Grid.
  • Select now matches the height of TextField and other inputs.
  • Badge now uses a pill shape on mobile.
  • Banner title contrast has been improved.
  • ColorPicker saturation-well shadow fixed at the corners.

Layout

  • On narrow screens, Section’s primary action moves below the card instead of squeezing the heading.
  • Section headings and subheadings now have tighter spacing.
  • Aside Section headings now use the default text color.
  • Menu icons use the secondary icon color at rest.
  • Page aside Section styling is fixed.
  • Page/Section secondary actions no longer lose their disclosure icon when their Menu or label is added after mount.
  • The first nested Section no longer sits lower than other first children.
  • Slotted actions no longer disappear when component markup is injected into an already-connected element.

Reliability, state and performance

  • GlobalThis.polaris state is no longer lost when a page loads the bundle more than once.
  • Modal actions now fire a bubbling click even with commandFor set.
  • TextField accessory clicks now reach React onClick handlers.
  • Faster mounting and updates, especially on pages without React, and less re-rendering from unrelated attribute changes on ChoiceList, Menu, Modal, Select, and pickers.

title: More control over commerce updates with Next Gen Events
summary:
With the 2026-10 API version Next Gen Events, Shopify's successor to classic webhooks, is now generally available. Events give you more customization than classic webhooks, letting you choose what changes your app receives, and what data comes with the payload.

If your app keeps track of collection memberships, for example, finding out that a collection changed is only part of the work. You still need to know which product joined or left. With classic webhooks, that can mean fetching the collection's products, comparing them with your saved list, and then updating your app. You're doing all of that work to identify one change.

We built Events to make this easier. Your subscription tells us which changes your app cares about and what data it needs to process them. We send you the change, the affected resource IDs, and the result of your GraphQL query together.

Tell us what your app cares about

You configure Events subscriptions right in your app's shopify.app.toml configuration file. An event has three components:

  • triggers: Which changes matter to your app. For example, a product joining or leaving a collection, or a variant's price changing.
  • query: What data you need when that happens. Write a GraphQL Admin API query, and we'll include its result in the payload. You can include related data and metafields too.
  • query_filter: Which results your app needs to receive. For example, you can limit deliveries to only products with an ACTIVE status.

The trigger and query are independent. A change to one field can trigger a query that fetches the other data your app needs. The query filter then checks that result to decide whether to deliver it. For more on how triggers, queries, and query filters work together, see the Events overview.

Receive the change and the data you need together

Let's continue to use collection memberships as an example. Your app maintains a search index, and you need to update it whenever a product joins or leaves a collection.

You can subscribe to collection.products and use the collection and product IDs directly in your query:

[events]
api_version = "2026-10"

[[events.subscription]]
handle = "collection-membership"
topic = "Collection"
actions = ["update"]
triggers = ["collection.products"]
uri = "/api/events/collections"

query = """
  query CollectionMembership($collectionId: ID!, $productsId: ID!) {
    collection(id: $collectionId) {
      id
      hasProduct(id: $productsId)
    }
  }
"""

When product 456 is added to collection 123, you receive a payload like this:

{
  "topic": "Collection",
  "action": "update",
  "handle": "collection-membership",
  "data": {
    "collection": {
      "id": "gid://shopify/Collection/123",
      "hasProduct": true
    }
  },
  "fields_changed": {
    "added": [
      "collection[id: 'gid://shopify/Collection/123'].products[id: 'gid://shopify/Product/456']"
    ],
    "updated": [],
    "removed": []
  },
  "query_variables": {
    "collectionId": "gid://shopify/Collection/123",
    "productsId": "gid://shopify/Product/456"
  }
}

Your app now knows which product joined which collection:

  • The action is update because adding a product changes the collection's membership.
  • The query tells you that hasProduct is true. That query runs as part of your subscription, so you don't need to make another API call after receiving the delivery or fetch the collection's full product list.
  • fields_changed.added tells you what changed.
  • query_variables gives you both IDs.

The query result reflects the state when the query runs, so use fields_changed to understand the change and data for the current context. The delivery structure guide has more examples.

More topics to build with

We started the developer preview with Product and Customer. We've expanded our coverage to many more key types across Admin GraphQL:

  • Merchandising: Product and Collection
  • Customers and companies: Customer and Company
  • Orders, fulfillment, and returns: Order, FulfillmentOrder, Refund, and Return
  • Inventory and locations: InventoryItem, InventoryShipment, InventoryTransfer, and Location
  • Content: Article, Blog, and Page
  • Custom data: MetafieldDefinition, Metaobject, and MetaobjectDefinition

Each topic has its own supported triggers, query variables, and access scopes. Check the Events API reference for the changes you want to subscribe to.

Get more out of your subscriptions

It can be tempting to copy your existing payload into a GraphQL query and subscribe to every change. That gets you familiar data, but it also carries over a lot of the work your app was already doing.

Start with what your app needs to do when something changes, then shape the subscription around that. In the collection example, we only need the affected membership. Loading every product in the collection on each delivery adds work without helping us process that change.

The Events optimization guide walks through choosing specific triggers, querying the affected resource, and splitting subscriptions while keeping the data your app needs. It also explains the complexity limit Shopify places on your queries and how to check that your queries stay within that limit before releasing your configuration.

As you move over to Events from classic webhooks, measure the deliveries your app receives, the size of each payload, and the follow-up API calls it makes. Those will tell you where the change is helping and where there's more work to do.

Get started

Your existing classic webhook integrations will continue to work. You can use both in the same app and move workflows over one at a time. For topics or subscription patterns Events doesn't support yet, keep using classic webhooks.

  • Moving from Webhooks to Events?: We recommend starting with identifying a workflow where your app is receiving a lot of updates and discarding most of them, or making another API call on every delivery. Look at what your handler actually does, which changes it needs, and what data it reads. That gives you the starting point for your subscription. Check out the migration guide to get started.
  • Brand new to both classic webhooks and Events?: To get started, use Shopify CLI version 4.83 or later and follow the getting started guide. Set your events API version to 2026-10 and choose the topic and triggers your app needs from the reference.
  • Already using the Events developer preview? Just update your events API version from unstable to 2026-10, including any subscription-level overrides. Review the versioned topic reference, then test and deploy the updated configuration.

We'd love to hear what you build with events, and where you're getting stuck. If a missing topic or trigger is blocking your migration, tell us which workflow you're trying to move over in the developer community.

It can be tempting to copy your existing payload into a GraphQL query and subscribe to every change. That gets you familiar data, but it also carries over a lot of the work your app was already doing.

Start with what your app needs to do when something changes, then shape the subscription around that. In the collection example, we only need the affected membership. Loading every product in the collection on each delivery adds work without helping us process that change.

The Events optimization guide walks through choosing specific triggers, querying the affected resource, and splitting subscriptions while keeping the data your app needs. It also explains the complexity limit Shopify places on your queries and how to check that your queries stay within that limit before releasing your configuration.

As you move over to Events from classic webhooks, measure the deliveries your app receives, the size of each payload, and the follow-up API calls it makes. Those will tell you where the change is helping and where there's more work to do.

Your existing classic webhook integrations will continue to work. You can use both in the same app and move workflows over one at a time. For topics or subscription patterns Events doesn't support yet, keep using classic webhooks.

  • Already using the Events developer preview? Just update your events API version from unstable to 2026-10, including any subscription-level overrides. Review the versioned topic reference, then test and deploy the updated configuration.

We'd love to hear what you build with events, and where you're getting stuck. If a missing topic or trigger is blocking your migration, tell us which workflow you're trying to move over in the developer community.

title: Discounts can now be included in Rollouts
summary:
Update your app to account for discount Rollouts

Summary

Admin GraphQL API version 2026-10 adds a read-only rollouts connection across Discount types. Apps that read discounts should use Discount.rollouts alongside existing discount fields to account for Rollout-driven schedules and buyer reach.

What's changing

Merchants can include discounts in Rollouts to coordinate launches, test discounts with a share of buyers, or run temporary events alongside other store changes. When a discount is part of a Rollout, its native dates alone don't describe its availability.

Update your integration

  • Request access. Add read_rollouts to your app's scopes. Existing resource scopes still apply to the underlying resource payloads, and existing installations may need merchant reauthorization.
  • Read the discount's Rollouts. Query Discount.rollouts to identify which Rollouts affect the discount.
  • Combine schedules and availability data. Read Rollout schedule fields alongside the discount's existing startsAt and endsAt fields. Also read effective allocation, treatment splits, and whether each change activates or expires the discount. Configured traffic allocation alone does not determine effective reach.

Account for sales-channel availability

Discounts activated at 100% effective traffic are available across all sales channels, subject to normal discount eligibility rules. Partial-traffic Rollout activation applies on the Online Store only.

Discounts outside Rollouts behave as before.

Earlier API versions

On Admin GraphQL API versions earlier than 2026-10, discounts are filtered out if they are active but may not reach all buyers, or if their status differs from the status inferred from native dates.

See the Discount Rollouts upgrade guide for integration guidance and examples.

To discover Rollouts independently of a discount or receive notifications when they change, see Rollouts queries and webhooks in the Admin GraphQL API.

title: Orders webhooks now include selling_plan_id on line items
summary:
Line items in Orders webhook payloads now include a selling_plan_id field. This field identifies the selling plan applied to a subscription line item, which helps you avoid extra API calls to look up that information. The change applies to API version 2026-10 and later, and you don’t need to take any action to keep your app working.

Previously, if your app needed to know which selling plan applied to a subscription line item, it had to make a follow-up Admin API call for every order it received. That value now arrives directly in the webhook payload.

In Orders webhook payloads, selling_plan_id contains the ID of the selling plan applied to the line item. It’s null for line items that aren’t part of a subscription.

{
  "line_items": [

      "id": 123456789,
      "selling_plan_id": 987654321
    }
  ]
}

This example shows a line item that includes a selling_plan_id value for a subscription.

This change is available on API version 2026-10 and later. Earlier versions are unaffected, and no action is required.

title: New fiscalDeviceIdentifier field on PointOfSaleDevice
summary:
As of the 2026-10 GraphQL Admin API version, the PointOfSaleDevice object includes a new fiscalDeviceIdentifier field. This field returns the Shopify-assigned fiscal register identifier (manufacturing number) for a POS device. You only need to adopt it if your app supports in-person fiscal compliance workflows.

What changed

The PointOfSaleDevice object in the GraphQL Admin API now includes a nullable fiscalDeviceIdentifier field. It returns the Shopify-assigned fiscal register identifier for the device, for example Sweden's manufacturing number (tillverkningsnummer) that merchants register with the Swedish Tax Agency (Skatteverket). For details, see the PointOfSaleDevice reference.

The field returns a value only for devices at locations in countries whose fiscal regulations require registering the cash register with the tax authority. Sweden is the first supported country. For all other devices, the field returns null.

Who's affected

Apps that support in-person fiscal compliance workflows, such as fiscal transaction signing and journal reporting in countries that require registered cash registers, can use this field. Apps that don't work with POS fiscal compliance aren't affected and don't need to take action.

What to do

  1. Query the field on the 2026-10 GraphQL Admin API version:

    query {
  pointOfSaleDevice(id: "gid://shopify/PointOfSaleDevice/123") {
    fiscalDeviceIdentifier
  }
}

    This query returns the fiscal register identifier for the device, or null when the device's location doesn't require one.

  2. To identify the device that your POS UI extension is running on, use session.deviceId, available in POS UI Extensions API 2026-04 and later, and query the GraphQL Admin API with that ID.

  3. Treat the value as stable for the lifetime of the device registration, and cache it per device.

  • POS UI Extensions Session API

title: `metafieldInteger` collection condition removed in API version 2027-01
summary:
As of API version 2027-01, the metafieldInteger collection source condition inputs and types is removed from GraphQL Admin API. If you use metafieldInteger to create or read collection source conditions, you need to migrate to metafieldInt before you upgrade to API version 2027-01.

What changed

With metafieldInt, the value field on integer metafield conditions changes type from Int to String, to align with the metafield value field on the Storefront API. For details, see the Storefront Metafield.value field reference.

The following types and fields are replaced:

  • CollectionSourceInclusionConditionMetafieldInteger is replaced by CollectionSourceInclusionConditionMetafieldInt
  • CollectionSourceInclusionConditionMetafieldIntegerRelation is replaced by CollectionSourceInclusionConditionMetafieldIntRelation
  • CollectionSourceInclusionConditionInput.metafieldInteger is replaced by CollectionSourceInclusionConditionInput.metafieldInt
  • CollectionSourceInclusionConditionUpdateInput.metafieldInteger is replaced by CollectionSourceInclusionConditionUpdateInput.metafieldInt

The relation enum members are unchanged (EQUALS, GREATER_THAN, LESS_THAN). The behavioral difference is that value is now a String instead of an Int.

Writes

These examples show the required switch from metafieldInteger to metafieldInt and the change in the value literal type.

Before:

conditionsToCreate: [{
  metafieldInteger: { definitionId: "gid://shopify/MetafieldDefinition/1", relation: GREATER_THAN, value: 2000 }
}]

After:

conditionsToCreate: [{
  metafieldInt: { definitionId: "gid://shopify/MetafieldDefinition/1", relation: GREATER_THAN, value: "2000" }
}]

Reads

This example shows the updated type condition you need to use when you read collection source conditions.

Before:

... on CollectionSourceInclusionConditionMetafieldInteger { relation value }

After:

... on CollectionSourceInclusionConditionMetafieldInt { relation value }

Action required

Before you move to API version 2027-01, you need to:

  • Update all Admin GraphQL queries and mutations that reference metafieldInteger to use metafieldInt.
  • Ensure all integer metafield condition value fields are strings.

If you don’t update your app before you use API version 2027-01, mutations that send metafieldInteger fail validation, and queries that select CollectionSourceInclusionConditionMetafieldInteger return errors. You can test metafieldInt behavior on 2026-10 before you upgrade to 2027-01.

metafieldInteger continues to work on API versions up to and including 2026-10. On 2026-10, integer metafield conditions resolve to CollectionSourceInclusionConditionMetafieldInt when present. In API version 2027-01, metafieldInteger is no longer available.

  • Collection source inclusion condition update inputs
  • Collection source inclusion condition metafield Int type reference
  • GraphQL Admin API reference

title: Added parseWarnings to ShopifyqlQueryResponse
summary:
Starting in API version 2026-10, the shopifyqlQuery query in the GraphQL Admin API returns a new parseWarnings field on ShopifyqlQueryResponse. This field surfaces non-fatal issues, such as the use of fields scheduled for deprecation, so you can detect and address them proactively.

What changed

shopifyqlQuery now returns a parseWarnings field alongside your results. The field is always present: it returns a list of warning messages when a successful query has non-fatal issues, and an empty list when there are none.

Unlike parseErrors, which explain why a query failed to run, parseWarnings are only returned on queries that ran successfully, together with tableData. Warnings don’t block execution, but they highlight potential problems you should consider fixing.

Why this matters

Warnings help you identify and resolve issues before they cause failures, such as upcoming deprecations or other changes that could affect your queries in future API versions. By monitoring parseWarnings, you can keep your ShopifyQL queries compatible as the API evolves.

What to do

Add parseWarnings to your shopifyqlQuery selection set, and check it after a successful query in the same way you already check parseErrors:

query {
  shopifyqlQuery(query: "FROM sales SHOW total_sales SINCE -7d") {
    tableData { columns { name } rows }
    parseWarnings
    parseErrors
  }
}

In this example, parseWarnings will contain any non-fatal warnings related to the query, or an empty list if there are none.

  • ShopifyqlQueryResponse object
  • ShopifyQL query language
  • API versioning

title: The `orderCancel` mutation now returns a structured `jobResult`
summary:
As of the 2026-10 GraphQL Admin API version, the orderCancel mutation returns a new jobResult field of type OrderCancelJobResult.

Order cancellations run asynchronously. The jobResult field provides a structured, cancellation-specific result, including the cancellation status, any errors, and the affected order. Use this field to check whether the cancellation completed successfully and to handle any errors.

Previously, the mutation only exposed the generic job field, which didn’t include cancellation-specific status or errors. The existing job field is unchanged and continues to work as before, so no action is required for existing integrations.

title: Tax webhook summary and calculation requests now use Global IDs
summary:
Starting with API version 2027-01, third-party tax apps will receive Global IDs (GIDs) in tax calculation requests and tax summary webhook payloads for all entity references of the summary section. This aligns with how Partners interact with other Shopify APIs.

These apps can now use the same identifiers across all Shopify endpoints without managing different ID formats for tax-specific integrations.

What's changed

This change affects two key integration points:

Tax calculation requests:

  • Customer, Company, CompanyLocation, Product, and ProductVariant IDs now use the GID format.

Tax summary webhooks:

  • All entity IDs within the summary section (Order, Customer, Product, ProductVariant, SalesAgreement, Sale, LineItem, Company, CompanyLocation ShippingLine, and TaxLine) now use the GID format.
  • The webhook payload also includes new admin_graphql_api_id fields at the top level for TaxSummary, Shop, and Order entities.

Changes include:

  • Top Level: Adds shop_admin_graphql_api_id and order_admin_graphql_api_id fields (existing shop_id and order_id remain as integers).
  • Customer IDs: Changes from "id": "5" to "id": "gid://shopify/Customer/5".
  • Product IDs: Changes from "id": "1" to "id": "gid://shopify/Product/1".
  • Product Variant IDs: Changes from "id": "1" to "id": "gid://shopify/ProductVariant/1".
  • Line Item IDs: Changes from "line_item_id": "5" to "line_item_id": "gid://shopify/LineItem/5".
  • Sale IDs: Changes from "id": "9" to "id": "gid://shopify/Sale/9".
  • Agreement IDs: Changes from "id": "6" to "id": "gid://shopify/Agreement/6".
  • Company IDs: Changes from "id": "3" to "id": "gid://shopify/Company/3".
  • Company Location IDs: Changes from "id": "4" to "id": "gid://shopify/CompanyLocation/4".
  • Shipping Line IDs: Changes from "id": "4" to "id": "gid://shopify/ShippingLine/4".
  • Tax Line IDs: Changes from "id": 6 to "id": "gid://shopify/TaxLine/6".

What you need to do

Update your integrations to handle the GID format when processing tax calculations and webhook payloads in API version 2027-01 and later. The following are some examples:

Tax calculation request

Before (2026-10 and earlier): 

{
  "cart": {
    "buyer_identity": {
      "customer": {
        "id": "593934299"
      }
    }
  }
}

After (2027-01):

{
  "cart": {
    "buyer_identity": {
      "customer": {
        "id": "gid://shopify/Customer/593934299"
      }
    }
  }
}

Tax summary webhook

Before (2026-10 and earlier):

{
  "id": 80,
  "shop_id": 1,
  "order_id": 64,
  "summary": {
    "agreements": [{
      "id": "82",
      "sales": [{
        "id": "106",
        "line_item_id": "76"
      }]
    }]
  }
}

After (202-01):

{
  "id": 80,
  "admin_graphql_api_id": "gid://shopify/TaxSummary/80",
  "shop_id": 1,
  "shop_admin_graphql_api_id": "gid://shopify/Shop/1",
  "order_id": 64,
  "order_admin_graphql_api_id": "gid://shopify/Order/64",
  "summary": {
    "agreements": [{
      "id": "gid://shopify/SalesAgreement/82",
      "sales": [{
        "id": "gid://shopify/Sale/106",
        "line_item_id": "gid://shopify/LineItem/76"
      }]
    }]
  }
}

  • The webhook payload also includes new admin_graphql_api_id fields at the top level for TaxSummary, Shop, and Order entities.

Changes include:

  • Top Level: Adds shop_admin_graphql_api_id and order_admin_graphql_api_id fields (existing shop_id and order_id remain as integers).
  • Customer IDs: Changes from "id": "5" to "id": "gid://shopify/Customer/5".
  • Product IDs: Changes from "id": "1" to "id": "gid://shopify/Product/1".
  • Product Variant IDs: Changes from "id": "1" to "id": "gid://shopify/ProductVariant/1".
  • Line Item IDs: Changes from "line_item_id": "5" to "line_item_id": "gid://shopify/LineItem/5".
  • Sale IDs: Changes from "id": "9" to "id": "gid://shopify/Sale/9".
  • Agreement IDs: Changes from "id": "6" to "id": "gid://shopify/Agreement/6".
  • Company IDs: Changes from "id": "3" to "id": "gid://shopify/Company/3".
  • Company Location IDs: Changes from "id": "4" to "id": "gid://shopify/CompanyLocation/4".
  • Shipping Line IDs: Changes from "id": "4" to "id": "gid://shopify/ShippingLine/4".
  • Tax Line IDs: Changes from "id": 6 to "id": "gid://shopify/TaxLine/6".

What you need to do

Update your integrations to handle the GID format when processing tax calculations and webhook payloads in API version 2027-01 and later. The following are some examples:

Tax calculation request

Before (2026-10 and earlier): 

{
  "cart": {
    "buyer_identity": {
      "customer": {
        "id": "593934299"
      }
    }
  }
}

After (2027-01):

{
  "cart": {
    "buyer_identity": {
      "customer": {
        "id": "gid://shopify/Customer/593934299"
      }
    }
  }
}

Tax summary webhook

Before (2026-10 and earlier):

{
  "id": 80,
  "shop_id": 1,
  "order_id": 64,
  "summary": {
    "agreements": [{
      "id": "82",
      "sales": [{
        "id": "106",
        "line_item_id": "76"
      }]
    }]
  }
}

After (202-01):

{
  "id": 80,
  "admin_graphql_api_id": "gid://shopify/TaxSummary/80",
  "shop_id": 1,
  "shop_admin_graphql_api_id": "gid://shopify/Shop/1",
  "order_id": 64,
  "order_admin_graphql_api_id": "gid://shopify/Order/64",
  "summary": {
    "agreements": [{
      "id": "gid://shopify/SalesAgreement/82",
      "sales": [{
        "id": "gid://shopify/Sale/106",
        "line_item_id": "gid://shopify/LineItem/76"
      }]
    }]
  }
}

title: New SubscriptionContractCalculation API for subscription management
summary:
A new SubscriptionContractCalculation API is now available to manage subscriptions. This new API runs subscription contract edits through Shopify's checkout engine, enabling new capabilities:

  • Shopify Functions, including cart transforms and delivery customizations are supported during contract calculations
  • Contract edits align with what the subscriber sees during billing
  • Get a preview of the full calculated contract (totals, delivery options, and warnings) before persisting any changes

Developers using the SubscriptionDraft API should migrate to SubscriptionContractCalculation API. The SubscriptionDraft API will remain available but will not support the new capabilities.

See the migration guide and updated subscriptions build guides and API docs.

title: Inventory shipment webhooks include inventory transfer IDs
summary:
We are introducing the inventory_transfer_id to several inventory_shipment webhook payloads to make it easier for developers to identify which inventory_transfer records, if any, a given shipment is related to. This will ease integration burdens and remove the need for developers to merge the datasets on their end to manually build the links.

What changed

Introduces an inventory_transfer_id field to the payloads of the following...

  • inventory_shipments/create
  • inventory_shipments/delete
  • inventory_shipments/add_items
  • inventory_shipments/remove_items
  • inventory_shipments/update_item_quantities
  • inventory_shipments/mark_in_transit
  • inventory_shipments/receive_items
  • inventory_shipments/update_tracking

Who's affected

This is an additive change, any adopters of the shipment webhooks, upon updating to 2026-10, will get access to this new field.

title: Updated function syntax on the segment query language
summary:
As of GraphQL Admin API version 2026-10, functions in the segment query language now use the operators MATCHES/NOT MATCHES instead of = true/= false. For example, the previous query shopify_email.opened() = true would now be represented as shopify_email.opened MATCHES ().

The parameters for each function have also been expanded to use their own operators. For example, the query products_purchased(quantity: 5) = true would now be represented as products_purchased MATCHES (quantity = 5). This expands the functionality of parameters. For example, the following queries were not possible before: products_purchased MATCHES (quantity != 5), products_purchased MATCHES (quantity > 5).

Additionally, the following named dates have been deprecated: 12_months_ago, 90_days_ago, 30_days_ago, 7_days_ago. Instead, the you can use the existing date offsets in your segment queries. For example, the named date 12_months_ago is equivalent to the date offset -12m.

Learn more about customer segment filters in our Help Center.
